title: Toeplitz Block Mixing for Scalable Multi-Head Linear Attention

raw.stage1:
### Purpose:
The purpose of the contribution is to show that the full \( M \times M \) block mixing matrix in Multi-Head Linear Attention (MHLA) is over-parameterized. None of the prior papers explicitly establish or report this specific empirical relationship. While some papers (e.g., [1], [5], [11], [13]) discuss redundancy or inefficiencies in multi-head attention mechanisms, they focus on different aspects, such as head redundancy, parameter sharing, or low-rank approximations, rather than directly addressing over-parameterization in the block mixing matrix of MHLA. No prior work demonstrates or empirically establishes this specific over-parameterization.

### Mechanism:
The mechanism involves fitting the learned MHLA mixing matrices to a distance-tied (translation-invariant) kernel to show that coefficients depend primarily on relative block distance. Paper [3] discusses translation-invariant kernels for multivariable approximation, which is conceptually equivalent to the use of a distance-tied kernel in this contribution. The underlying primitive — using translation-invariant kernels to model relationships — is shared, even though [3] applies it in a different context (function approximation and classification tasks).

### Evaluation:
The evaluation demonstrates that the distance-tied kernel fit yields \( R^2 > 0.995 \) across all layers. This is a specific instance of fitting a kernel model and reporting a high \( R^2 \) value as a measure of fit quality. Paper [3] also evaluates the suitability of translation-invariant kernels for approximation tasks, though it does not report \( R^2 \) specifically. However, the evaluation design — fitting a kernel model and validating its performance — is conceptually equivalent. Thus, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain:
The domain is efficient attention/sequence modeling. Papers such as [2], [4], [5], [9], and [11] all operate in the same general application area of efficient attention mechanisms or sequence modeling. While the specific focus on MHLA and its block mixing matrix is unique to this contribution, the broader domain of efficient attention is well-covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to remove the O(M²) block-mixing bottleneck of MHLA and enable extrapolation to longer sequences. Paper [1] explicitly addresses the quadratic complexity bottleneck in self-attention mechanisms and proposes linear attention methods to overcome it, which aligns with the same problem-class level objective. Paper [17] also targets the quadratic complexity issue in Transformers and introduces a neural architecture for efficient sequence modeling with unlimited context length, which similarly aims to enable extrapolation to longer sequences. Both papers share the same purpose at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces Toeplitz Block Mixing (TBM), which parameterizes the mixing kernel as a mixture of exponentials \( K(\delta) = \sum_r a_r \exp(-\lambda_r \delta) \), constraining mixing to depend only on block distance. Paper [12] uses a similar mechanism of approximating linear combinations of integral kernels with exponential sums, expressing non-local terms as auxiliary variables. Paper [11] also discusses Toeplitz matrices and kernel parameterization, specifically noting exponential decay behavior in learned kernels. Both papers employ substantively equivalent primitives involving exponential kernel parameterization and Toeplitz structures.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates the reduction in mixing complexity from \( O(M²d²) \) to \( O(MRd²) \) for kernel rank \( R \ll M \) and demonstrates length extrapolation due to the kernel's definition for any distance. Paper [1] evaluates linear attention methods by comparing computational complexity and sequence length scalability, which matches the evaluation design of complexity reduction and extrapolation validation. Paper [17] similarly evaluates sequence modeling architectures for efficiency and extrapolation to longer contexts, using comparable metrics and validation setups. Both papers reuse the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of linear attention architectures. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], and [17] all work within the general application area of linear attention architectures, addressing various aspects of efficiency, scalability, and expressiveness. While the specific sub-problems differ, the domain remains the same.
